questions.stem: Many excavations of the 18th and 19th centuries are criticised by archaeologists today. Which is the main reason?
options: Diggers recorded every layer in such detail that their reports cannot be understood
Diggers refused to remove any objects, leaving them exposed to the weather
Diggers sought fine objects and often failed to record where they lay
Diggers used scientific dating methods that have since been shown to be unreliable
questions.explanation: Early excavation was often treasure hunting for collectors and museums, so the context of finds was lost. Scientific dating methods such as radiocarbon came only in the mid 20th century.

questions.stem: Flinders Petrie, working in Egypt from the 1880s, is regarded as a founder of scientific archaeology mainly because he:
options: recorded all finds, even ordinary pottery, and used them to build a sequence
invented radiocarbon dating and used it to fix the dates of Egypt's earliest kings
was the first to dig in Egypt with permission from the Egyptian government
excavated only royal tombs, ignoring settlement sites as of little value
questions.explanation: Petrie valued everyday objects as evidence and developed sequence dating (seriation) from changes in pottery styles. Radiocarbon dating was developed by Willard Libby in the late 1940s.

questions.stem: The basic principle of stratigraphy is that, in undisturbed deposits:
options: lower layers were laid down before the layers above them
the thickest layers always represent the longest periods
objects of gold are always found in the deepest layers
each layer represents exactly one century of occupation
questions.explanation: The law of superposition means deeper layers are older, giving a relative sequence. Layer thickness depends on how fast material built up, not on time alone.

questions.stem: Radiocarbon dating could be used on which of these finds?
options: A granite statue carved for a temple courtyard
A gold coin minted for a Persian king
Charred seeds from a hearth in an ancient house
A bronze sword found buried beside a warrior
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of carbon-14 in material that was once alive, such as seeds, wood, bone or textiles. Metal and stone contain no organic carbon from a living thing.

questions.stem: Which dating method would be most suitable for a fired clay pot with no organic remains?
options: Dendrochronology
Radiocarbon dating
Potassium-argon dating
Thermoluminescence
questions.explanation: Thermoluminescence measures energy stored in minerals since they were last heated, such as when clay was fired. Dendrochronology needs tree rings, radiocarbon needs organic material, and potassium-argon dates volcanic rock over very long periods.

questions.stem: Strontium isotope analysis of teeth from a burial shows that a woman grew up far from the place where she was buried. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: She was buried during a time of plague or famine
She was a foreign slave brought in by the local king
She moved to the area at some point after childhood
She died in a battle fought far from her homeland
questions.explanation: Strontium in tooth enamel reflects the geology of the area where a person lived as a child, so a mismatch shows movement. On its own it cannot reveal why she moved or her status.

questions.stem: Technologies such as LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar and satellite imagery are increasingly used by archaeologists. Their main advantage is that they:
options: can recover the DNA of people buried at a site from the air above it
can replace excavation completely, so sites never need to be dug again
can reveal buried features without digging and destroying them
can date objects precisely without the need for any laboratory tests
questions.explanation: Remote sensing maps features under vegetation or soil without disturbing them, helping archaeologists decide where, or whether, to dig. It does not date objects, and excavation is still needed to test what is found.

questions.stem: Archaeologists often say that 'excavation is destruction'. What does this mean for how a site must be investigated?
options: Once layers are dug away they cannot be re-examined, so recording must be thorough
Excavation always damages objects, so nothing found should ever be removed from a site
Excavation should be done quickly so that weather has little time to damage the site
Excavation is now illegal, so archaeologists rely on written sources instead
questions.explanation: Digging removes the layers and context that give finds their meaning, so the excavation record becomes the only evidence. This is why many sites are now left partly unexcavated for future methods.

questions.stem: The Piltdown Man, 'discovered' in England in 1912, was exposed as a hoax in 1953. How was the fraud shown?
options: Radiocarbon dating proved that the bones were less than ten years old
Tests showed the bones were of different ages and had been stained
A written confession by the finder was found in a museum archive after his death
DNA testing showed that the skull belonged to a modern chimpanzee from Africa
questions.explanation: Scientific tests showed a human skull and an orangutan's jaw, stained to look old, with the teeth filed down. DNA analysis of the remains came much later, and the bones were not a single creature at all.

questions.stem: In 1896 the Louvre bought a gold 'Tiara of Saitaphernes', said to be ancient Greek. In 1903 it was shown to be modern. What does the case best show about authentication?
options: Museums are never fooled because they buy only from known excavations
Style is the only reliable test of whether an object is ancient or not
Experts can be deceived, so provenance and testing are needed
Gold objects can never be forged, so the tiara must have been ancient
questions.explanation: The tiara was made by a goldsmith in Odessa, and its style fooled experts until its maker was identified. Checking where an object came from and testing its materials guard against forgeries.

questions.stem: The Getty kouros, a Greek-style marble statue bought by the J. Paul Getty Museum in the 1980s, is still labelled as either ancient or a modern forgery. Why has the question not been settled?
options: It is carved from a stone that did not exist in the ancient Greek world
Its excavation records show it was found in a Roman layer, not a Greek one
Experts disagree on its style and scientific tests have not given a clear answer
The museum has refused to allow anyone to examine the statue since it was bought
questions.explanation: The statue mixes stylistic features from different periods, documents of its history proved false, and tests on its marble surface have been inconclusive. It has no record of excavation, which is part of the problem.

questions.stem: At most ancient sites, stone, pottery and metal survive far better than wood, textiles and food. What is the main effect of this on our picture of the past?
options: Our view is skewed towards the poor, who used more stone than the rich
Our view is accurate, since organic materials are always found in tombs
Our view is skewed towards durable materials and the activities that used them
Our view is complete, since organic materials were rarely used in ancient times
questions.explanation: Differential preservation means much of what people made and used has decayed, except in dry, frozen, waterlogged or buried-by-eruption conditions. Organic materials were very widely used.

questions.stem: An archaeologist finds a richly furnished grave and declares it the tomb of a king. Which is the best reason for caution?
options: Grave goods are always placed by robbers, so they reveal nothing about the dead
Burials cannot be studied scientifically, so all conclusions are guesses
Rich goods show status, but not a specific office without other evidence
Rich graves always belong to priests, since kings were buried with few goods
questions.explanation: Archaeological evidence shows what was buried, but identifying the person's role usually needs inscriptions or other context. Interpretation goes beyond what the objects show directly.

questions.stem: Most works of Greek and Roman historians survive only in manuscripts copied centuries after they were written. What problem does this create?
options: The texts were translated into Greek from Latin and lost their meaning
The originals were all written on stone, so the copies must be invented
The copies were made by the ancient authors themselves, so they are biased
Copying errors, gaps and changes may have entered the text over time
questions.explanation: Texts passed through many hands, and scribes could miss lines, misread words or add notes. Scholars compare manuscripts to reconstruct the most likely original.

questions.stem: Royal inscriptions such as the Behistun inscription of Darius I or the Res Gestae of Augustus are valuable but must be used carefully because they:
options: present the ruler's own version of events for public display
were written by enemies of the ruler to damage his reputation
were carved by ordinary people who had no knowledge of events
were written many centuries after the events they describe
questions.explanation: These inscriptions were carved on the ruler's orders, so they show how he wished to be seen, stressing successes and leaving out failures. They are close in time to events, which is part of their value.

questions.stem: Petroglyphs are images carved into rock. Which is a major limitation of petroglyphs as a source?
options: They always show events in order, so they cannot be interpreted in different ways
They were painted over by later peoples, so none of the original images survive
They are hard to date, and their meaning may depend on cultural knowledge we lack
They were made only by kings, so they show nothing about ordinary people
questions.explanation: Rock carvings rarely contain datable material, and they may have had meanings known only to those who made them or their descendants. Many survive in remarkably good condition.

questions.stem: In Egyptian art the king is often shown far larger than the people around him. A historian interpreting such iconography should recognise that:
options: size showed importance, following convention rather than real height
Egyptian kings were chosen because they were taller than other people
artists measured each figure carefully to record its true size
the smaller figures were children, not adults, in all of these scenes
questions.explanation: Hierarchical scale was a convention in which size showed status. Images have to be read with an understanding of the conventions and purposes of the art.

questions.stem: Much of the ancient picture of Cleopatra VII as a dangerous seductress comes from Roman writers. Why must historians treat this image carefully?
options: It was invented in the 20th century by Hollywood film studios
It was shaped by the propaganda of Octavian, her enemy in war
It was written by Cleopatra's own courtiers to flatter the queen
It comes from Egyptian temple inscriptions carved after her death
questions.explanation: Octavian presented his war against Antony as a war against a foreign queen, and later Roman writers echoed this view. Modern films drew on these ancient accounts rather than inventing the image.

questions.stem: The film 300 shows the Spartans at Thermopylae as defenders of freedom and the Persians as monstrous. Which statement best explains why such representations differ from the evidence?
options: They follow Herodotus exactly, adding nothing of their own
They are made by historians, so they must be fully accurate
They reflect the values and purposes of their own time and audience
They are based on newly found Persian sources unknown to historians
questions.explanation: Representations are shaped by when, why and for whom they were made, such as entertainment or modern political concerns. Herodotus gives a far more varied picture of the Persians.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to evaluate a modern representation of an ancient person, such as a statue, film or novel?
options: Compare it with ancient sources and ask who made it, when and why
Accept it if it is popular, since many people have approved of it
Reject it at once, since no representation can contain any truth
Judge it only on how realistic its costumes and settings look
questions.explanation: Evaluating a representation means checking it against the evidence and considering its creator's context and purpose. Representations can be valuable evidence of later attitudes even when inaccurate.

questions.stem: The image of Alexander the Great has changed over time, from heroic conqueror to ruthless tyrant. Which is the strongest explanation?
options: Alexander changed his own image by writing several different autobiographies
Each period reads limited, biased sources in light of its own values
New eyewitness accounts of Alexander's life are found every few decades
Ancient sources agree completely, so the changes come only from novels
questions.explanation: The main surviving accounts were written centuries after his death from lost sources, so there is room for interpretation. Changing views about empire and war shape how historians read them.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a human threat to the survival of an ancient site?
options: Salt rising through walls from groundwater
Mass tourism wearing down floors and paintings
Erosion of stone by wind-blown sand over centuries
Earthquakes damaging walls and columns
questions.explanation: Tourism is a human threat, along with looting, war, pollution and development. Wind erosion, earthquakes and rising salts are natural processes, though human activity can worsen some of them.

questions.stem: In the 1960s the temples of Abu Simbel were cut into blocks and rebuilt on higher ground. Why?
options: An earthquake had cracked the cliff into which they were cut
The government wanted them closer to Cairo for visitors
The lake behind the Aswan High Dam would have flooded them
Tourists had damaged the original site beyond repair
questions.explanation: An international campaign led by UNESCO moved the temples to save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser. They were moved a short distance uphill, not to Cairo.

questions.stem: The Venice Charter of 1964 is an international guide to conserving monuments. Which practice does it support?
options: Rebuilding missing parts to look exactly as the restorer imagines them
Painting ruins in bright colours so visitors can picture them as new
Removing later additions from every site to show only its first phase
Reassembling fallen original pieces, with new material clearly marked
questions.explanation: The charter allows anastylosis, putting existing pieces back in place, and says restoration should stop where guesswork begins. Additions must be recognisable as modern.

questions.stem: Australia's Burra Charter, first adopted in 1979 by Australia ICOMOS, guides heritage conservation. Its central principle is to:
options: rebuild damaged places using modern materials so they last longer
change a place only as much as necessary and otherwise as little as possible
restore every heritage place to look exactly as it did when it was first built
leave all heritage places untouched, even if they are collapsing
questions.explanation: The charter takes a cautious approach that respects the existing fabric and its significance. It does not demand full restoration or forbid all intervention.

questions.stem: Arthur Evans rebuilt parts of the palace at Knossos in the 1920s using reinforced concrete. Why is this reconstruction controversial?
options: It mixed guesswork with original remains and is now hard to undo
It used only original materials, so visitors cannot tell what is new
It was based on Linear B tablets that Evans had wrongly translated
It moved the palace to a new site to protect it from earthquakes
questions.explanation: Evans's reconstructions shape how visitors picture the Minoans, but parts reflect his interpretations, and the concrete itself now needs conservation. Linear B was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, after Evans's death.

questions.stem: The Lascaux cave in France was closed to the public in 1963, and a replica cave was later opened nearby. What does this show about conservation?
options: Closing a site always ends the risk of damage to its paintings
Visitors cause no harm if they are not allowed to touch the walls
Replicas let people experience a site while protecting the original
Replicas are built only after an original site has been totally destroyed
questions.explanation: Visitors' breath, heat and the light they brought changed the cave's climate and harmed the paintings, so access was closed. Replicas balance public access with protection, though problems in the original cave continued.

questions.stem: After the Arch of Triumph at Palmyra was destroyed in 2015, a scaled replica made with 3D modelling was displayed in London and other cities. Which is the best evaluation of such digital reconstructions?
options: They make conservation unnecessary, since any site can now be printed again
They are worthless, since only original stone has any historical value
They prove that the original arch was never really destroyed in the war
They record and share lost heritage, but cannot replace the original
questions.explanation: Digital models preserve information and raise awareness, and can guide repairs, but the original's age and authenticity cannot be recreated. They work alongside conservation, not instead of it.

questions.stem: After the fall of Baghdad in April 2003, the Iraq Museum was looted. Why is looting such a serious loss for historians, even if objects are later recovered?
options: Records and context are lost, and sites lose evidence of where finds lay
Recovered objects are always forgeries, so they can no longer be studied
Looted objects are always destroyed and melted down for their metal
Recovered objects must by law be kept in storage and never displayed
questions.explanation: Looting of sites destroys context, and theft from museums scatters objects and records. Many objects from the Iraq Museum were returned, but damage to sites and archives cannot be undone.

questions.stem: The 1970 UNESCO Convention is important in the trade in antiquities because it:
options: banned archaeology in countries that had been colonies
aims to stop the illegal import and export of cultural property
made it legal for museums to buy any antiquity offered for sale
required all museums to return every object from overseas
questions.explanation: The convention set an international standard against illicit trade, and many museums now require proof that an object left its country before 1970 or legally. It did not require the return of everything.

questions.stem: Museums do more than display objects. Which activity is a central role of a museum?
options: Conserving and storing collections in controlled conditions
Selling artefacts to private collectors to fund excavations
Keeping collections secret to protect them from scholars
Restoring all objects to look new before they are shown
questions.explanation: Museums acquire, conserve, research and exhibit collections, keeping temperature, humidity and light controlled. Selling to private collectors and hiding collections run against museum ethics.

questions.stem: The Parthenon sculptures were removed from Athens on Lord Elgin's orders in the early 19th century and are now in the British Museum. Which argument is made FOR their return to Greece?
options: The British Museum has no space to display them and keeps them in storage
They were made in Britain and taken to Greece, so they should come back
Greek law requires all ancient sculpture to stay in the country where it was found
They belong to one monument and to Greek identity, and could be shown near it
questions.explanation: Supporters of return stress cultural identity and reuniting the sculptures with the rest of the frieze in the Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009. The British Museum displays them and argues it acquired them legally.

questions.stem: Some large museums argue against repatriation by calling themselves 'universal museums'. What is the core of this argument?
options: Objects are always safer in the country where they were made
Displaying objects from many cultures together serves people worldwide
Objects in museums belong to no one, so no nation has any claim to them
Repatriation is illegal under all international conventions since 1970
questions.explanation: Universal museums argue that world collections let visitors compare cultures and that objects are well cared for. Critics reply that many items were taken in unequal colonial conditions.

questions.stem: A gallery of ancient objects shows mostly gold jewellery, royal statues and temple treasures. Which question about 'whose past is represented' does this raise?
options: Whether gold objects should be replaced with modern copies
Whether the display neglects ordinary people, women and the enslaved
Whether the objects are too old to be of interest to visitors
Whether the museum should display only objects from its own country
questions.explanation: Displays often favour elite, valuable or beautiful objects, which can give a narrow view of the past. Museums increasingly try to show everyday life and a wider range of voices.

questions.stem: Tollund Man, found in a Danish peat bog in 1950, is remarkably well preserved because:
options: his body was embalmed with natron and resin by Iron Age priests
the body was frozen in glacier ice until it was found by walkers
volcanic ash buried him and set hard around his body
cold, acidic, low-oxygen water slowed decay and tanned the skin
questions.explanation: Bog conditions limit bacteria and tan the skin, although the acids dissolve much of the bone. Freezing in ice preserved Ötzi, and ash preserved bodies at Pompeii.

questions.stem: Ötzi, the man found in the Alps in 1991 who lived over 5,000 years ago, was later shown by X-ray to have:
options: a gold crown hidden under his fur hood
a tattoo naming the village where he lived
a skull fracture made during mummification
a stone arrowhead in his left shoulder
questions.explanation: An X-ray in 2001 revealed the arrowhead, showing he was shot shortly before he died. He was naturally preserved by ice, not mummified by people.

questions.stem: Why do researchers now often use CT scanning to study mummified remains rather than unwrapping them?
options: It removes the wrappings safely so they can be displayed
It shows what lies inside the wrappings without damage
It dates the remains more precisely than any other method
It is the only way to extract DNA from very old remains
questions.explanation: Scanning is non-invasive and produces 3D images of what lies under the wrappings. Unwrapping, common in the 19th century, destroyed evidence and the remains themselves.

questions.stem: The Chinchorro people of northern Chile and southern Peru are significant in the study of human remains because they:
options: were the first people to use radiocarbon dating on their dead
left no burials at all, so their remains have never been studied
buried their dead only in peat bogs like those of northern Europe
practised artificial mummification long before the Egyptians
questions.explanation: The Chinchorro began deliberately preparing their dead about 5000 BCE, long before the earliest known Egyptian mummification. Their remains show complex beliefs about death.

questions.stem: A museum is deciding whether to display a mummified body. Which consideration best reflects current ethical thinking?
options: Whether the person was royal, since only royal remains need to be respected
The person's beliefs, descendants' views and respectful presentation
Whether the display will attract more visitors than other parts of the museum
Whether the remains are complete enough to be put on show without repairs
questions.explanation: Ethical guidelines ask museums to treat remains as people, consider the wishes of descendants or source communities, and display them with dignity, or not at all. Status does not change the obligation.

questions.stem: Laws such as the United States' Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (1990) are significant because they:
options: allow museums to buy human remains from any country without restriction
ban all scientific study of human remains more than a century old
require all human remains in museums to be cremated within a year
require institutions to return certain remains and sacred objects
questions.explanation: The law set up a process for returning remains and sacred objects to descendant communities. It reflects a wider shift in which communities, not institutions alone, decide how remains are treated.
